rv.q: “The Snow Geese” doesn’t dig deep, but there’s something satisfying about its shamelessly old-fashioned approach: Oedipal tension! Feuding brothers! Families overwhelmed by the times! A war that will change everything!
Too bad the play lets them all down.
It’s a pretty but unsatisfying meal, undercooked and overstuffed.
White’s dull, emotionally uninvolving attempt to do the same with America lacks thematic weight.
Despite these infelicities, The Snow Geese makes you care about this flawed and fractious clan.
And if his first act is slow to take off, he's got the ideal company to ensure a heartfelt landing.
But in time, "The Snow Geese," as directed by Daniel Sullivan with his characteristic polish, turns into the atmospheric character study that White intended.
Whatever the problem may be, it leaves this Snow Geese foundering.
'The Snow Geese,' which opened Thursday night at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, has a refreshingly unusual setting: a hunting lodge near Syracuse in 1917.
Director Daniel Sullivan, as always, can’t help but put on a good show, aided here by John Lee Beatty’s stupendous set that miraculously converts from dining room to kitchen to sylvan pond.
There is little heart in the matter.
